I've been working this land my whole life, learned from my father and grandfather. My farm is small — 4.1 mu — and I have to be careful because some family members are working in town. I can't afford to lose a season.

My land splits roughly like this: about 2.5 mu goes into the wheat-maize rotation, and the other 1.6 mu I keep in cotton. That's how I've always done it here in Quzhou. Cotton brings cash income, and wheat-maize feeds the family and covers feed costs.

**Wheat:** I'll buy improved seeds from the township supply cooperative, same brand as last year. I sow in early October. I know I need to water three times — the wintering water before freeze, again at jointing, and once at heading. No point in fancy calculations, that's just what keeps the grain full. I'll put down compound fertilizer at sowing and topdress urea at jointing. I rotary-till after the maize comes off in October to break up the stubble before sowing.

**Maize:** Right after I harvest wheat in June, I direct-seed maize into the stubble. No-till saves me labor because my family is short-handed with people working off-farm. I use hybrid seed — everyone around here does, the yields are much better. I'll fertilize twice: at sowing and again when it's knee-high. I water when the tassels come out if it's dry.

**Cotton:** I plough this plot in spring, transplant seedlings in late April. Cotton is the most work — I have to spray for bollworm and aphids several times through summer. I water it when the bolls are setting. This is my cash crop so I can't slack on it.
